criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one pending measure, marked), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.

entries.title: The CARES Act (March 2020)
entries.explainer: The first pandemic relief law: $1,200 payments to most adults, expanded unemployment benefits, and forgivable loans to keep small businesses paying staff.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary
entries.senateSearch: Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security

entries.title: The American Rescue Plan (March 2021)
entries.explainer: The second big pandemic package: $1,400 payments, an expanded child tax credit that paid parents monthly for a year, and money for vaccines, schools and state governments.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (2021)
entries.explainer: About $550 billion in new money for roads, bridges, water pipes, rural broadband and the electric grid, spread over five years.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (2022)
entries.explainer: The first major federal gun law in about 30 years — tougher checks for buyers under 21, money for state red-flag programs and school mental health. Still in effect; the under-21 provisions expire in 2032 by the law's own terms.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: The CHIPS and Science Act (2022)
entries.explainer: About $52 billion to pay companies to build computer-chip factories in the United States, after the pandemic showed how much depends on chips made elsewhere.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: The Honoring our PACT Act (2022)
entries.explainer: Extended VA health care and disability benefits to veterans exposed to burn pits and other toxic hazards, and made the government presume certain illnesses were service-related instead of making each veteran prove it.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: The Inflation Reduction Act (2022)
entries.explainer: Let Medicare negotiate the price of some prescription drugs and capped insulin at $35 a month for people on Medicare, alongside tax credits for clean energy, paid for partly by a minimum tax on large corporations.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: The Respect for Marriage Act (2022)
entries.explainer: Requires every state to recognize same-sex and interracial marriages performed in other states, so those marriages stay valid even if the Supreme Court changes course.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: The Fiscal Responsibility Act (2023)
entries.explainer: Ended the debt-ceiling standoff by suspending the borrowing limit into 2025, in exchange for caps on federal spending and new work requirements for some food-stamp recipients.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: April 2024: aid to Ukraine
entries.explainer: About $61 billion for Ukraine's defense against Russia's invasion — weapons, ammunition, and economic support.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: April 2024: aid to Israel and humanitarian aid for Gaza
entries.explainer: About $26 billion for Israel's military and air defenses, including roughly $9 billion for humanitarian relief in Gaza and other conflict zones.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: April 2024: Indo-Pacific and Taiwan
entries.explainer: About $8 billion for military support to Taiwan and other allies in the Indo-Pacific, and for U.S. submarine production.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: April 2024: TikTok divest-or-ban, and sanctions
entries.explainer: Required TikTok's Chinese owner to sell the app or have it blocked in U.S. app stores, and added sanctions on Russia, Iran and their weapons suppliers.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: The Social Security Fairness Act (2025)
entries.explainer: Repealed two rules that reduced Social Security for millions of retired teachers, police, and other public workers, raising their monthly benefits.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: The Laken Riley Act (2025)
entries.explainer: Requires federal immigration authorities to detain people in the country illegally who are arrested for theft or certain violent crimes, and lets states sue the federal government over immigration enforcement decisions.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)
entries.explainer: Made the 2017 income-tax rates permanent and added new deductions, while cutting Medicaid and food-stamp spending through tighter eligibility and work rules, and increasing immigration-enforcement funding.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: The GENIUS Act (2025)
entries.explainer: The first federal rulebook for stablecoins — digital tokens meant to hold a fixed dollar value — requiring issuers to hold real dollar reserves and submit to federal or state supervision.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: The shutdown and the 2026 appropriations that ended it
entries.explainer: Reopened the federal government after the longest shutdown on record and funded it for the rest of the year, restoring back pay to federal workers and resuming paused federal payments.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (2025)
entries.explainer: The first broad federal housing law in years: money and rule changes aimed at getting more homes built, plus changes to rental assistance and homelessness programs.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary

entries.title: Banning members of Congress from trading individual stocks
entries.explainer: Would bar members of Congress, and in most versions their spouses, from buying and selling individual company shares while in office, requiring blind trusts or divestment instead.
entries.explainerSource: congress.gov bill text and official summary
entries.senateNote: The Senate hasn't voted on this. It passed the House and is waiting.

entries.title: Amy Coney Barrett to the Supreme Court
entries.explainer: A lifetime seat on the Supreme Court, filled eight days before the 2020 election after Justice Ginsburg's death.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Xavier Becerra as Secretary of Health and Human Services
entries.explainer: The department that runs Medicare, Medicaid and the public-health agencies, confirmed in the middle of the pandemic.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Deb Haaland as Secretary of the Interior
entries.explainer: The department that manages federal public land, national parks and relations with tribal nations; she is the first Native American cabinet secretary.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Alejandro Mayorkas as Secretary of Homeland Security
entries.explainer: The department that runs border enforcement, immigration services, disaster response and the Coast Guard.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Merrick Garland as Attorney General
entries.explainer: The head of the Justice Department, which decides which federal crimes are prosecuted and defends federal law in court.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Janet Yellen as Secretary of the Treasury
entries.explainer: The department that manages federal borrowing, tax collection and sanctions policy.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Pete Buttigieg as Secretary of Transportation
entries.explainer: The department that regulates airlines, railroads and highway safety and distributes federal transport money.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Jerome Powell for a second term as Chair of the Federal Reserve
entries.explainer: The Federal Reserve sets interest rates, which is the main lever anyone in government has over inflation and unemployment.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Ketanji Brown Jackson to the Supreme Court
entries.explainer: A lifetime seat on the Supreme Court; she is the first Black woman to serve on it.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Pete Hegseth as Secretary of Defense
entries.explainer: The department that commands the armed forces and spends roughly half of all money Congress appropriates each year. The Senate split 50-50 and the Vice President broke the tie.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as Secretary of Health and Human Services
entries.explainer: The department that runs Medicare, Medicaid, the FDA and the CDC, including federal vaccine policy.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Tulsi Gabbard as Director of National Intelligence
entries.explainer: The official who oversees all eighteen federal intelligence agencies and decides what the President is told.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Kash Patel as Director of the FBI
entries.explainer: A ten-year term running the federal government's main criminal and counter-intelligence investigators.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Pam Bondi as Attorney General
entries.explainer: The head of the Justice Department, which decides which federal crimes are prosecuted and defends federal law in court.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Marco Rubio as Secretary of State
entries.explainer: The department that conducts foreign policy, runs the embassies and issues visas. Confirmed unanimously.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.

entries.title: Todd Blanche as Deputy Attorney General
entries.explainer: The second-ranking official at the Justice Department, who runs its day-to-day operations and supervises the U.S. Attorneys.
entries.explainerSource: senate.gov roll-call record; the office's own statutory description
entries.houseNote: The House doesn't vote on nominations.
